title: Adwoa and the Missing Market Change

pages.text: On Saturday morning, Mama handed eight-year-old Adwoa a crisp twenty-cedi note and a woven basket. ‘Please go to Auntie Dede’s stall,’ said Mama. ‘Buy three bunches of kontomire, one bowl of tomatoes, and one pack of salt. Count the prices and your change carefully.’
sentences: On Saturday morning, Mama handed eight-year-old Adwoa a crisp twenty-cedi note and a woven basket.
‘Please go to Auntie Dede’s stall,’ said Mama.
‘Buy three bunches of kontomire, one bowl of tomatoes, and one pack of salt.
Count the prices and your change carefully.’
pages.alt: Mama hands Adwoa a crisp twenty-cedi note and a woven basket in their sunny courtyard.

pages.text: At the market, Adwoa went straight to Auntie Dede’s stall. First, she picked three fresh green bunches of kontomire leaves. Each bunch cost two cedis. Adwoa counted in twos on her fingers: ‘Two, four, six. Three bunches cost six cedis.’
sentences: At the market, Adwoa went straight to Auntie Dede’s stall.
First, she picked three fresh green bunches of kontomire leaves.
Each bunch cost two cedis.
Adwoa counted in twos on her fingers: ‘Two, four, six.
Three bunches cost six cedis.’
pages.alt: At the market stall, Adwoa holds three bunches of green kontomire leaves and counts on her fingers.

pages.text: Next, Auntie Dede measured one bowl of shiny red tomatoes for five cedis. Adwoa added the numbers in her head: ‘Six cedis for the kontomire plus five cedis for the tomatoes makes eleven cedis.’
sentences: Next, Auntie Dede measured one bowl of shiny red tomatoes for five cedis.
Adwoa added the numbers in her head: ‘Six cedis for the kontomire plus five cedis for the tomatoes makes eleven cedis.’
pages.alt: Auntie Dede pours shiny red tomatoes from a metal bowl into Adwoa’s basket.

pages.text: Last of all, Adwoa picked up one small pack of salt for three cedis. She added three cedis to eleven cedis: ‘Twelve, thirteen, fourteen! Everything in my basket costs fourteen cedis in all.’
sentences: Last of all, Adwoa picked up one small pack of salt for three cedis.
She added three cedis to eleven cedis: ‘Twelve, thirteen, fourteen!
Everything in my basket costs fourteen cedis in all.’
pages.alt: Adwoa places a small white pack of salt into her basket beside the tomatoes and kontomire.

pages.text: Adwoa worked out her change before handing over the twenty-cedi note. ‘Twenty cedis minus fourteen cedis leaves six cedis,’ she whispered. ‘So I should get six cedis change.’
sentences: Adwoa worked out her change before handing over the twenty-cedi note.
‘Twenty cedis minus fourteen cedis leaves six cedis,’ she whispered.
‘So I should get six cedis change.’
pages.alt: Adwoa holds out her twenty-cedi note to Auntie Dede while several customers crowd around the stall.

pages.text: Three noisy customers were asking Auntie Dede for onions at the same time. In the rush, Auntie Dede took Adwoa’s twenty-cedi note and quickly pressed two five-cedi notes into Adwoa’s hand. ‘Thank you, little one!’ called Auntie Dede.
sentences: Three noisy customers were asking Auntie Dede for onions at the same time.
In the rush, Auntie Dede took Adwoa’s twenty-cedi note and quickly pressed two five-cedi notes into Adwoa’s hand.
‘Thank you, little one!’ called Auntie Dede.
pages.alt: In a busy rush with other shoppers, Auntie Dede hands two five-cedi notes to Adwoa.

pages.text: Under the shade of a neem tree, Adwoa stopped and looked at her hand. Five cedis plus five cedis was ten cedis! ‘Wait,’ said Adwoa. ‘My change should be six cedis, not ten cedis. Ten minus six is four. Auntie Dede gave me four cedis too much!’
sentences: Under the shade of a neem tree, Adwoa stopped and looked at her hand.
Five cedis plus five cedis was ten cedis!
‘Wait,’ said Adwoa.
‘My change should be six cedis, not ten cedis.
Ten minus six is four.
Auntie Dede gave me four cedis too much!’
pages.alt: Under a shady tree, Adwoa looks at the two five-cedi notes in her palm with wide, thoughtful eyes.

pages.text: For a moment, Adwoa saw a seller with sweet yellow mangoes nearby. Four extra cedis could buy two juicy mangoes! Then she thought of how hard Auntie Dede worked in the sun every day. Adwoa turned right around and walked back to the stall.
sentences: For a moment, Adwoa saw a seller with sweet yellow mangoes nearby.
Four extra cedis could buy two juicy mangoes!
Then she thought of how hard Auntie Dede worked in the sun every day.
Adwoa turned right around and walked back to the stall.
pages.alt: Adwoa glances past a tray of yellow mangoes and walks determinedly back toward Auntie Dede’s stall.

pages.text: ‘Auntie Dede,’ said Adwoa, ‘my items cost fourteen cedis, so my change from twenty cedis is six cedis. You gave me ten cedis by mistake.’ Auntie Dede counted again, clapped her hands in gratitude, and exchanged one five-cedi note for a one-cedi coin. ‘Six cedis exact!’ she beamed. ‘You are a sharp mathematician and an honest child.’ The end.
sentences: ‘Auntie Dede,’ said Adwoa, ‘my items cost fourteen cedis, so my change from twenty cedis is six cedis.
You gave me ten cedis by mistake.’ Auntie Dede counted again, clapped her hands in gratitude, and exchanged one five-cedi note for a one-cedi coin.

pages.alt: Auntie Dede smiles warmly and gives Adwoa her exact six cedis change as Adwoa beams with pride.
